name: Combining Qualitative and Quantitative Data
title: Combining Qualitative and Quantitative Data
answer: Combining qualitative and quantitative data covers research designs that bring narrative, textual, or observational material together with numeric measures, counts, or model outputs. In AI research this often means pairing interview transcripts, field notes, or open-ended survey responses with performance metrics, error rates, or demographic statistics. The aim is to explain not only what a system does but why and for whom, and to check findings across different kinds of evidence. Mixed methods work sits between purely interpretive qualitative analysis and purely statistical quantitative analysis, and it is used in evaluation, user research, and social studies of AI.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Combining qualitative and quantitative data covers research designs that bring narrative, textual, or observational material together with numeric measures, counts, or model outputs. In AI research this often means pairing interview transcripts, field notes, or open-ended survey responses with performance metrics, error rates, or demographic statistics. The aim is to explain not only what a system does but why and for whom, and to check findings across different kinds of evidence. Mixed methods work sits between purely interpretive qualitative analysis and purely statistical quantitative analysis, and it is used in evaluation, user research, and social studies of AI.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on standard research computing rather than any single specialised stack. Qualitative data is usually managed in coding software or plain text files with annotation layers, while quantitative data lives in statistical packages, spreadsheets, or databases. Integration often happens in scripts written in Python or R that join coded segments to numeric records by participant or case identifier. Increasingly, language model pipelines are used to suggest codes or summarise long text, but the core infrastructure remains a version-controlled dataset with clear links between source quotes and their numeric counterparts.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A common approach is a convergent design, where qualitative and quantitative strands are collected separately and then merged during interpretation. Another is a sequential design, where one strand informs the other, for example using interviews to explain an unexpected drop in a metric or using survey results to select cases for close reading. Analysts often convert qualitative codes into counts or presence indicators, a step called quantitizing, and they may also group numeric patterns into narrative profiles. Joint displays, tables that place quotes beside statistics for the same cases, are a standard way to make the integration visible and checkable.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on the provenance of both kinds of data and on the people behind them. Qualitative material often contains identifiable detail, so consent, anonymisation, and secure storage are central, and re-identification risk rises when quotes are linked to quantitative attributes. Mixed methods work should record how codes were assigned, which analyst coded which segment, and how numeric variables were defined, so that an outside reviewer can trace a claim back to its source. Bias can enter at the point of sampling, coding, or merging, and a finding that looks robust in one strand may be an artefact of how the two datasets were joined.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more systematic and partly automated integration. Language models are being used to propose codes, extract structured variables from text, and draft joint displays, though human review remains the norm for high-stakes interpretation. Researchers are also working on standards for reporting mixed methods studies in AI, including templates for joint displays and audit trails. Multimodal data, such as screen recordings, speech, and interaction logs, is likely to be combined with survey and interview material more often, and there is growing interest in using qualitative findings to interrogate quantitative model evaluations rather than simply supplement them.
